Conserved developmental networks underlie post-embryonic remodelling in teleosts

28 July 2026

1 Introduction

Comparative embryology has revealed that early animal development is based on highly conserved genetic programs. Beyond embryogenesis however, animals undergo remarkably diverse post-embryonic developmental transitions such as metamorphosis. Whether these transitions are also organised into conserved genetic programs remains largely unexplored. To identify conserved genetic programs underlying post-embryonic development, we examine metamorphic remodelling in five teleost fishes, spanning 200 million years of evolution. By integrating comparative co-expression networks, evolutionary genomics, phylogenetic modelling, and functional data in zebrafish, we uncovered a conserved post-embryonic developmental network. This conserved network comprises components involved in core cellular processes, and involved in development and physiology, both of which are under the control of thyroid hormone during metamorphosis. Despite evolutionary conservation at the coding sequence level, this network exhibits significant turnover in gene family copy number following the teleost-specific whole-genome duplication as well as lineage-specific expansions and contractions. The variation in gene copy numbers is associated with macroevolutionary variation in a number of ecological and morphological traits, including swimming performance, and trophic level. Cross-species tissue expression, zebrafish single-cell transcriptomics, and zebrafish perturbation phenotypes placed the implicated genes in biological contexts relevant to these traits. Together, our results provide evidence of an ancient, functionally partitioned post-embryonic developmental network that has diversified throughout teleost evolution. The heterochronic variation in network function, changes in endocrine activity, and gene-family turnover provide potential routes through which a shared developmental architecture contributed to the evolution of phenotypic diversity in teleosts. 2 Getting ortholog expression matrix

Since the goal of this project is to identify core sets of genes mediating metamophorosis across different species of fish I need to estimate the orthologs between the genes and construct networks of the orthologous genes. For that I need to construct an ortholog gene expression matrix. I estimate orthlogs using OrthoDB and filter out only the genes families that are present in all 5 species. This step ensures we select gene families that have a common evolutionary history, and not ones that have species-specific evolutionary trajectories (either gains or losses).

orth<-readRDS("./04.Orthogroups/Orthologer_latest2.rds") 

rbind(
rbind(
  orth %>% filter(str_detect(orths,"ENSAOCG")),
  orth %>% filter(str_detect(orths,"ENSDARG"))) %>% 
  mutate(orths= str_remove(orths,"\\.[0-9]*")) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Orthogroup,orths,sp),
rbind(
    orth %>% filter(str_detect(orths,"Goby")),
    orth %>% filter(str_detect(orths,"Grouper")),
    orth %>% filter(str_detect(orths,"Manini")))  %>%
  dplyr::select(Orthogroup,orths,sp))->metamorph_orthlist

full_orths<-metamorph_orthlist %>% summarise(n = n(),.by = c(Orthogroup,sp)) %>% summarise(n = n(),.by = c(Orthogroup)) %>% filter(n == 5)

#Get clown orths
left_join(clown$dge_keep$counts %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("orths"),
          metamorph_orthlist %>% filter(str_detect(orths, "ENSAOCG"))) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup) %>% drop_na() %>% distinct(orths,.keep_all = T)->clown_orth_exp

#Get grouper orths
left_join(grouper$dge_keep$counts %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("orths"),
          metamorph_orthlist %>% filter(str_detect(orths, "Grouper"))) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup) %>% drop_na()->grouper_orth_exp

#Get manini orths
left_join(manini$dge_keep$counts %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("orths"),
          metamorph_orthlist %>% filter(str_detect(orths, "Manini"))) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup) %>% drop_na()->manini_orth_exp

#Get goby orths
left_join(goby$dge_keep$counts %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("orths"),
          metamorph_orthlist %>% filter(str_detect(orths, "Goby"))) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup) %>% drop_na()->goby_orth_exp

#Get danio orths
left_join(danio$dge_keep$counts %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("orths"),
          metamorph_orthlist %>% filter(str_detect(orths, "ENSDARG"))) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup) %>% drop_na()->danio_orth_exp

2.1 Summarising expression across orthologs

Since there are typically multiple gene copies we decided to use the copy with the highest expression for each orthogroup. Our objective is not to check how individual gene copies are co-expressed (at lease not yet), but rather get insight into the general co-expression of genes with similar functions. In this regard, choosing the gene copy with the highest expression will generally capture the most predominant signal and expression trends. The following piece of code shows that there is almost no difference in general expression trends when representing ortholog expression by using summary measure like mean, median, or summed expression and when selecting the ortholog with the highest expression.

#Randomly picks genes with multiple copies and displays summary metrics; users can try other fish and change the higher range of the runif
check_orth_exp_sumarries(exp_dat = clown_orth_exp,
                         a = (clown_orth_exp %>% janitor::get_dupes(Orthogroup) %>% distinct(Orthogroup))[runif(n = 1,min = 1,max =1835),1],
                         b = (clown_orth_exp %>% janitor::get_dupes(Orthogroup) %>% distinct(Orthogroup))[runif(n = 1,min = 1,max =1835),1])

2.2 Making ortholog expression matrix

In this step I process the gene expression matrices to obtain a one-to-one orthogroup expression matrix. This resulted in a gene expression matrix of 12,700 genes for each species. This matrix represents an orthologous expression matrix composed of the same gene families in all five species, which differ by their expression patterns across post-embryonic development in each species. Here you can see the clownfish matrix with genes as rows and samples as columns.

#Making ortholog matix
#Clown
clown_orth_exp %>% distinct(orths,.keep_all = T) %>% rowwise(orths) %>% 
           mutate(m=mean(Sample1:Sample21)) %>% ungroup() %>%  
           slice_max(m,by = "Orthogroup") %>% distinct(orths,.keep_all = T) %>% 
  distinct(Orthogroup,.keep_all = T)->clown_orth_exp
cln<-clown_orth_exp %>% dplyr::select(-c(orths,Orthogroup,sp,m)) %>% as.matrix()
colnames(cln)<-paste0(clown$dge_keep$samples$group, rep(".clown",length(clown$dge_keep$samples$group)))
clown_orth_exp_mat<-cbind(orths.clown = clown_orth_exp$orths, Orthogroup = clown_orth_exp$Orthogroup,
                      cln %>% as.data.frame())
#Grouper

  distinct(Orthogroup,.keep_all = T)->grouper_orth_exp

colnames(gbb)<-paste0(goby$dge_keep$samples$group, rep(".goby",length(goby$dge_keep$samples$group)))

#Danio
danio_orth_exp %>% distinct(orths,.keep_all = T) %>% rowwise(orths) %>%

purrr::reduce(list(goby_orth_exp_mat %>% dplyr::select(c(Orthogroup,orths.goby)),

3 Orthologus networks

We use Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) to construct the co-expression network of the developmental time-series data for each species. We construct the network for each species separately.

3.1 Soft threshold

This step estimates the power to achieve the scale free topology of the data. Choosing a soft threshold power for the developmental time-series data is not straight forward due to the dynamic nature of the gene expression. Therefore, I chose a power that balances the scale free nature of the data and it’s mean connectivity to ensure that I don’t get too sparse networks. I pick the power that has a scale-free R2 of at least 0.8.

soft_threshold(clown_orth_net_in$wgcna_in)->sft_clown_orth_net#pick 13 
soft_threshold(grouper_orth_net_in$wgcna_in)->sft_grouper_orth_net #pick 13
soft_threshold(goby_orth_net_in$wgcna_in)->sft_goby_orth_net #pick 12
soft_threshold(manini_orth_net_in$wgcna_in)->sft_manini_orth_net #pick 13
soft_threshold(danio_orth_net_in$wgcna_in)->sft_danio_orth_net #pick 13

rbind(sft_clown_orth_net$fitIndices %>% mutate(sp="clown"),
      sft_grouper_orth_net$fitIndices %>% mutate(sp="grouper"),
      sft_goby_orth_net$fitIndices %>% mutate(sp="goby"),
      sft_manini_orth_net$fitIndices %>% mutate(sp="manini"),
      sft_danio_orth_net$fitIndices %>% mutate(sp="danio")) %>% dplyr::select(sp,Power,SFT.R.sq,mean.k.,median.k.,max.k.,Density) %>% filter(SFT.R.sq>0.8 & median.k.>10) %>% saveRDS("./RDS/softThres_orth_net.rds")
soft<-readRDS("./RDS/softThres_orth_net.rds") 
soft %>% 
  kableExtra::kbl() %>% 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), 
                            full_width = F, 
                            position = "left") %>%
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "500px", height = "400px")

3.2 Making the networks

This step constructs the network.

#Clown
wgcna_adjacency(datExpr = clown_orth_net_in$wgcna_in, power = 13)->clown_orth_net

#Grouper
wgcna_adjacency(datExpr = grouper_orth_net_in$wgcna_in, power = 13)->grouper_orth_net

#Goby
wgcna_adjacency(datExpr = goby_orth_net_in$wgcna_in, power = 12)->goby_orth_net

#Manini
wgcna_adjacency(datExpr = manini_orth_net_in$wgcna_in, power = 13)->manini_orth_net

#Danio
wgcna_adjacency(datExpr = danio_orth_net_in$wgcna_in, power = 13)->danio_orth_net

clown_orth_net %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/clown_orth_net.rds")
grouper_orth_net %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/grouper_orth_net.rds")
goby_orth_net %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/goby_orth_net.rds")
manini_orth_net %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/manini_orth_net.rds")
danio_orth_net %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/danio_orth_net.rds")

3.3 Load the networks

I load the computed co-expression networks.

clown_orth_net<-readRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/clown_orth_net.rds")
grouper_orth_net<-readRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/grouper_orth_net.rds")
goby_orth_net<-readRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/goby_orth_net.rds")
manini_orth_net<-readRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/manini_orth_net.rds")
danio_orth_net<-readRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/danio_orth_net.rds")

3.4 Network stats

We see that the networks have almost the same number of modules. This is expected since the gene expression matrix has same number of orthogroups and the soft thresholds were similar. There is slight variation in the average module size and mean connectivity with zebrafish having the lowest average module size, while clownfish modules have the lowest average connectivity.

tibble(Species=c("Clonwfish","Grouper","Goby","Manini","Zebrafish"),
       Number_of_modules=c(length(clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)),
                           length(grouper_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)),
                           length(goby_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)),
                           length(manini_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)),
                           length(danio_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module))),
       
       Median_module_size=c(clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% median(),
                             grouper_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% median(),
                             goby_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% median(),
                             manini_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% median(),
                             danio_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% median()),
       
       Mean_mod_size=c(clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% mean() %>% round(),
                             grouper_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% mean() %>% round(),
                             goby_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% mean() %>% round(),
                             manini_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% mean() %>% round(),
                             danio_orth_net$connectivity %>% summarise(m=n(),.by = "module") %>% pull(m) %>% mean()) %>% round(),
       
       Mean_connectivity=c(mean(clown_orth_net$connectivity$degree) %>% round(3),
                           mean(grouper_orth_net$connectivity$degree) %>% round(3),
                           mean(goby_orth_net$connectivity$degree) %>% round(3),
                           mean(manini_orth_net$connectivity$degree) %>% round(3),
                           mean(danio_orth_net$connectivity$degree) %>% round(3))) %>% 
  kableExtra::kbl() %>% 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), 
                            full_width = F, 
                            position = "left")

4 Finding homologous modules

4.1 Module preservation

To quantify similarities between the post-embryonic co-expression networks I estimated module preservation statistics, which measure how well network properties are conserved between a reference and a test network. I performed pairwise comparisons of the network properties among all species. Since the networks were constructed using a one-to-one orthologous gene expression matrix, the estimate of module preservation tells us whether gene interactions during post-embryonic development in one species resemble another species.
The Zsummary score is used to denote the degree of preservation with scores above 10 typically used as evidence of high preservation and scores below 2 as evidence of no preservation. To get more reliable estimates I use more stringent thresholds to categorise preservation, with Zsummary > 12 as evidence of high preservation, Zsummary < 12 as evidence for low to medium preservation, and Zsummary < 6 as no evidence for preservation.

## Module preservation analysis
#In this step I check whether the co-expression modules identified in one species are preserved in another species. 

#For clownfish and grouper
setLabels = c("clown", "grouper");
multiExpr = list(clown = list(data = clown_orth_net_in$wgcna_in), 
                 grouper = list(data = grouper_orth_net_in$wgcna_in));
multiColor = list(clown = clown_orth_net$moduleColors$moduleColors, 
                  groper = grouper_orth_net$moduleColors$moduleColors);
nSets = 2

mp = modulePreservation(multiExpr, multiColor,
referenceNetworks = c(1:2),
nPermutations = 200,
randomSeed = 1,
verbose = 3)
mp %>% saveRDS("./02.Gene_expression_and_network/orth_module_pres_clownfish_grouper.rds")

4.2 Degree of preservation

rbind(
mp_plot_clown_ref_grouper$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>%  mutate(comp="Clowfish~Grouper"),
mp_plot_clown_ref_goby$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Clowfish~Goby"),
mp_plot_clown_ref_manini$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Clowfish~Manini"),
mp_plot_clown_ref_danio$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Clowfish~Danio"),
mp_plot_grouper_ref_clown$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Grouper~Clownfish"),
mp_plot_grouper_ref_goby$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Grouper~Goby"),
mp_plot_grouper_ref_manini$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Grouper~Manini"),
mp_plot_grouper_ref_danio$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Grouper~Danio"),
mp_plot_goby_ref_clown$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Goby~Clownfish"),
mp_plot_goby_ref_grouper$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Goby~Grouper"),
mp_plot_goby_ref_manini$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Goby~Manini"),
mp_plot_goby_ref_danio$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Goby~Danio"),
mp_plot_manini_ref_clown$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Manini~Clownfish"),
mp_plot_manini_ref_grouper$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Manini~Grouper"),
mp_plot_manini_ref_goby$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Manini~Goby"),
mp_plot_manini_ref_danio$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Manini~Danio"),
mp_plot_danio_ref_clown$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Danio~Clownfish"),
mp_plot_danio_ref_grouper$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Danio~Grouper"),
mp_plot_danio_ref_goby$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Danio~Goby"),
mp_plot_danio_ref_manini$dat %>% distinct(mods, .keep_all = T) %>% mutate(comp="Danio~Manini")
) %>% 
  dplyr::count(pres, comp) %>% 
  mutate(comp=reorder(comp, -n)) %>%  
  ggplot(aes(y=comp, x=n))+
    facet_wrap(~pres)+
  geom_col(aes(fill=pres), color="grey20", linewidth=0.2, position = "stack")+
    geom_text(aes(label=n, x=n-1.2), color="white", size=3)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#497BB6", "#B6497B", "#7BB649"))+
  labs(x="Comparisons", y="Number of modules")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle=0,size=8,hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size=8),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95"))

The following plots show the Jaccard indices for all the module comparisons with the significant higher than expected overlaps marked in red. I pick the module pairs with the highest Jaccard similarity and classify them as the conserved ones. Those are highlighted with black outline. The preservation classification is on the x and y axis. You can see that most homologous modules are usually highly preserved.

4.2.1 Clownfish and goby

#clown:317
#Grouper:310
#Goby:363
#Manini:385
#Zebrafish:385

expand_grid(c1=(clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)), 
            c2=(goby_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)))->jac_input

# Run the function with the ability to specify net1 and net2
purrr::map2(.x = jac_input$c1, 
            .y = jac_input$c2,  
            ~ get_jaccard_estimate(.x, .y, 
                                   net1 = clown_orth_net$moduleColors, 
                                   net2 = goby_orth_net$moduleColors)) %>% list_rbind() %>% 
  arrange(desc(jaccard_index))->membership_stats

#Reorder colums and adjust the pvalues
membership_stats %>% mutate(col.goby=reorder(c2,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
  mutate(col.clown=reorder(c1,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
  mutate(padj=p.adjust(membership_stats$f.test.pval,"BH"))->membership_stats

#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_clown_ref_goby$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.clown=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.clown",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(clown.pres=pres, stages.clown=stages, mod.z.clown=mod.z)->membership_stats
#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_goby_ref_clown$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.goby=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.goby",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(goby.pres=pres, stages.goby=stages, mod.z.goby=mod.z) ->membership_stats

membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.clown, col.goby, jaccard_index, padj, clown.pres, goby.pres)) %>% 
  mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
  padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.clown=reorder(col.clown,-jaccard_index))->membership_stats2

full_join(membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.clown, col.goby, jaccard_index, padj, clown.pres, goby.pres)) %>%
             mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
               padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.clown=reorder(col.clown,-jaccard_index)),
           membership_stats2 %>% filter(sig_ovelap == "yes") %>% 
             mutate(homo=case_when(
               jaccard_index >= quantile(membership_stats$jaccard_index,0.75) & sig_ovelap == "yes" ~ "homologous",
               .default = "non-homologous")) %>% 
     distinct(col.clown,col.goby, .keep_all = T) %>% 
   slice_max(order_by = jaccard_index,by = col.clown,n = 2,) %>% dplyr::select(col.clown,col.goby,homo),by = c("col.clown","col.goby")) %>%
   replace_na(list(homo="non-homologous"))->membership_stats2
  
membership_stats2 %>%  
  ggplot(aes(x=col.goby, y=col.clown))+
  geom_tile(aes(fill=jaccard_index, color=homo, width=0.8, height=0.8), size=0.3)+
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  facet_grid(clown.pres~goby.pres,space = "free",scales = "free")+
  labs(x=NULL, y=NULL)+
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9,"Oranges"),limits=c(0,0.5))+
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black","white"))+
  ggnewscale::new_scale_color()+
  geom_point(aes(color = sig_ovelap),alpha=0.3,size=0.3,shape=8)+
  scale_color_manual(values = c("white","red3"))+
  theme_void()+
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "left",
        axis.text = element_blank())->p1

  
  membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.clown, col.goby, jaccard_index, padj, clown.pres, goby.pres,phase.x)) %>% mutate(col.clown=reorder(col.clown,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x=col.goby,y=1))+
    geom_tile(aes(fill=goby.pres))+
    facet_grid(cols = vars(goby.pres),space = "free",scales = "free")+

  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = rev(cols.clown(11)), limits = c(-qnt, qnt),
                       breaks = c(-qnt, 0, qnt), labels = c(paste0("<", round(-qnt)), "0", paste0(">", round(qnt))))+

4.2.2 Clownfish and grouper

#clown:317
#Grouper:310

expand_grid(c1=(clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)), 
            c2=(grouper_orth_net$connectivity %>% distinct(module) %>% pull(module)))->jac_input

# Run the function with the ability to specify net1 and net2
purrr::map2(.x = jac_input$c1, 
            .y = jac_input$c2,  
            ~ get_jaccard_estimate(.x, .y, 
                                   net1 = clown_orth_net$moduleColors, 
                                   net2 = grouper_orth_net$moduleColors)) %>% list_rbind() %>% 
  arrange(desc(jaccard_index))->membership_stats

#Reorder colums and adjust the pvalues
membership_stats %>% mutate(col.grouper=reorder(c2,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
  mutate(col.clown=reorder(c1,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
  mutate(padj=p.adjust(membership_stats$f.test.pval,"BH"))->membership_stats

#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_clown_ref_grouper$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.clown=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.clown",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(clown.pres=pres, stages.clown=stages, mod.z.clown=mod.z)->membership_stats
#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_grouper_ref_clown$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.grouper=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.grouper",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(grouper.pres=pres, stages.grouper=stages, mod.z.grouper=mod.z) ->membership_stats


membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.clown, col.grouper, jaccard_index, padj, clown.pres, grouper.pres)) %>% 
  mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
  padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.clown=reorder(col.clown,-jaccard_index))->membership_stats2

full_join(membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.clown, col.grouper, jaccard_index, padj, clown.pres, grouper.pres)) %>%
             mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
               padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.clown=reorder(col.clown,-jaccard_index)),
           membership_stats2 %>% filter(sig_ovelap == "yes") %>% 
             mutate(homo=case_when(
               jaccard_index >= quantile(membership_stats$jaccard_index,0.75) & sig_ovelap == "yes" ~ "homologous",
               .default = "non-homologous")) %>% 
     distinct(col.clown,col.grouper, .keep_all = T) %>% 
   slice_max(order_by = jaccard_index,by = col.grouper, n=2) %>% dplyr::select(col.clown,col.grouper,homo),by = c("col.clown","col.grouper")) %>%
   replace_na(list(homo="non-homologous"))->membership_stats2
  
membership_stats2 %>%  
  ggplot(aes(x=col.grouper, y=col.clown))+
  geom_tile(aes(fill=jaccard_index, color=homo, width=0.8, height=0.8), size=0.3)+
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  facet_grid(clown.pres~grouper.pres,space = "free",scales = "free")+
  labs(x=NULL, y=NULL)+

  geom_point(aes(color = sig_ovelap),alpha=0.3,size=0.3,shape=8)+

  theme_void()+

  arrange(desc(jaccard_index))->membership_stats

membership_stats %>% mutate(col.manini=reorder(c2,-jaccard_index)) %>%

          membership_stats, by = "col.grouper",relationship = "many-to-many") %>%

#Join with the heatmap data

membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.grouper, col.manini, jaccard_index, padj, grouper.pres, manini.pres)) %>%

 full_join(membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.grouper, col.manini, jaccard_index, padj, grouper.pres, manini.pres)) %>%

               padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.grouper=reorder(col.grouper,-jaccard_index)),

             mutate(homo=case_when(
               jaccard_index >= quantile(membership_stats$jaccard_index,0.75) & sig_ovelap == "yes" ~ "homologous",
               .default = "non-homologous")) %>%

   replace_na(list(homo="non-homologous"))->membership_stats2

                                   net1 = manini_orth_net$moduleColors,

  arrange(desc(jaccard_index))->membership_stats

#Reorder colums and adjust the pvalues
membership_stats %>% mutate(col.goby=reorder(c2,-jaccard_index)) %>% 
  mutate(col.manini=reorder(c1,-jaccard_index)) %>%

#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_manini_ref_goby$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.manini=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.manini",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(manini.pres=pres, stages.manini=stages, mod.z.manini=mod.z)->membership_stats
#Join with the heatmap data
full_join(mp_plot_goby_ref_manini$dat %>% dplyr::rename(col.goby=mods),
          membership_stats, by = "col.goby",relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::rename(goby.pres=pres, stages.goby=stages, mod.z.goby=mod.z) ->membership_stats

membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.manini, col.goby, jaccard_index, padj, manini.pres, goby.pres)) %>% 
  mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
  padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>%  mutate(col.manini=reorder(col.manini,-jaccard_index))->membership_stats2



 full_join(membership_stats %>% dplyr::select(c(col.manini, col.goby, jaccard_index, padj, manini.pres, goby.pres)) %>%
             mutate(sig_ovelap=case_when(
               padj < 0.05 ~ "yes", padj > 0.05 ~ "no")) %>% mutate(col.manini=reorder(col.manini,-jaccard_index)),
           membership_stats2 %>% filter(sig_ovelap == "yes") %>% 
             mutate(homo=case_when(
               jaccard_index >= quantile(membership_stats$jaccard_index,0.75) & sig_ovelap == "yes" ~ "homologous",
               .default = "non-homologous")) %>% 
     distinct(col.manini,col.goby, .keep_all = T) %>% 
   slice_max(order_by = jaccard_index,by = col.goby, n=2) %>% dplyr::select(col.manini,col.goby,homo),by = c("col.manini","col.goby")) %>%
   replace_na(list(homo="non-homologous"))->membership_stats2

  geom_tile(aes(fill = mod.z.goby), color = "grey80",) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = rev(cols.goby(11)), limits = c(-qnt, qnt),
                       breaks = c(-qnt, 0, qnt), labels = c(paste0("<", round(-qnt)), "0", paste0(">", round(qnt))))+
  labs(y=NULL, x="goby stages")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90,hjust = -0.005,vjust = 0.2),
                        strip.text = element_blank(),
                        strip.background = element_blank(),
                        panel.grid = element_blank(),
                        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
                        legend.position = "top")->p4
  
  qnt<-max(membership_stats$mod.z.danio)
  membership_stats %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = stages.danio,x = col.danio))+
  facet_grid(cols = vars(danio.pres),space = "free",scales = "free")+
  geom_tile(aes(fill = mod.z.danio), color = "grey80",) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = rev(cols.danio(11)), limits = c(-qnt, qnt),
                       breaks = c(-qnt, 0, qnt), labels = c(paste0("<", round(-qnt)), "0", paste0(">", round(qnt))))+
  labs(x=NULL, y="danio stages")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
                        strip.background = element_blank(),
                        panel.grid = element_blank(),
                        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
                        legend.position = "bottom")->p5
  
  
  
wrap_plots(p1,p3,p2,nrow = 2,ncol = 2, heights = c(1,0.05), widths = c(1, 0.05))->wrapped_plot_goby_danio
wrapped_plot_goby_danio

4.2.11 Extract homologous modules

Start in sequence with the largest pairs first.

#clown:317
#Grouper:310
#Goby:363
#Manini:385
#Zebrafish:385

inner_join(
  wrapped_plot_clown_manini[[1]][1] %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(data.sig_ovelap == "yes") %>%
    distinct(data.col.clown, data.col.manini, .keep_all = T) %>%
    dplyr::rename(col.clown=data.col.clown, 
                  col.manini=data.col.manini, 
                  jaccard.index.clown.manini=data.jaccard_index, 
                  clown.ref.pres.manini=data.clown.pres, 
                  manini.ref.pres.clown=data.manini.pres),
  
      wrapped_plot_clown_danio[[1]][1] %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(data.sig_ovelap == "yes") %>% distinct(data.col.clown, data.col.danio, .keep_all = T) %>% 
    dplyr::rename(col.clown=data.col.clown, 
                  col.danio=data.col.danio, 
                  jaccard.index.clown.danio=data.jaccard_index, 
                  clown.ref.pres.danio=data.clown.pres, 
                  danio.ref.pres.clown=data.danio.pres),
 by = "col.clown", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  
  inner_join(
     wrapped_plot_clown_goby[[1]][1] %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(data.sig_ovelap == "yes") %>% 
    distinct(data.col.clown, data.col.goby, .keep_all = T) %>% 
    dplyr::rename(col.clown=data.col.clown, 
                  col.goby=data.col.goby, 
                  jaccard.index.clown.goby=data.jaccard_index, 
                  clown.ref.pres.goby=data.clown.pres, 
                  goby.ref.pres.clown=data.goby.pres),
    by = "col.clown", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  
  inner_join(
    wrapped_plot_clown_grouper[[1]][1] %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(data.sig_ovelap == "yes")
    %>% distinct(data.col.clown, data.col.grouper, .keep_all = T) %>%
      dplyr::rename(col.clown=data.col.clown, 
                  col.grouper=data.col.grouper, 
                  jaccard.index.clown.grouper=data.jaccard_index, 
                  clown.ref.pres.grouper=data.clown.pres, 
                  grouper.ref.pres.clown=data.grouper.pres),
    by = "col.clown", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  dplyr::select(c(col.clown,
                  col.goby,
                  col.danio,
                  col.manini,
                  col.grouper,
                  jaccard.index.clown.goby,
                  jaccard.index.clown.danio,
                  jaccard.index.clown.manini,
                  jaccard.index.clown.grouper,
                  clown.ref.pres.goby,
                  clown.ref.pres.danio,
                  clown.ref.pres.manini,
                  clown.ref.pres.grouper,
                  goby.ref.pres.clown,
                  danio.ref.pres.clown,
                  manini.ref.pres.clown,
                  grouper.ref.pres.clown))->homologous_modules

homologous_modules %>% saveRDS("./RDS/homologous_modules.rds")
homologous_modules<-readRDS("./RDS/homologous_modules.rds")

5 Extract homologous gene lists

Use this to extract homologous genes list.

#combine all the jaccard similarities
rbind(
tibble(all_jac=homologous_modules$jaccard.index.clown.goby),
tibble(all_jac=homologous_modules$jaccard.index.clown.danio),
tibble(all_jac=homologous_modules$jaccard.index.clown.manini),
tibble(all_jac=homologous_modules$jaccard.index.clown.grouper))->all_jac

#long version of data
homologous_modules %>% pivot_longer(contains("col"), names_to = "species.col", values_to = "col") %>% 
  pivot_longer(contains("jaccard"), names_to = "jaccard.comp", values_to = "jaccard.val") %>% 
  pivot_longer(contains("pres"),names_to = "pres.comp", values_to = "pres.val")->homologous_long

#filter out the top 30% homologous module comparisons
homologous_long %>% filter(jaccard.val >= quantile(all_jac$all_jac,0.70)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(species.col, col) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = species.col, values_from = col) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(col.goby, col.danio, col.manini, col.grouper, col.clown)) %>% 
  distinct(col.goby, col.danio, col.manini, col.grouper, col.clown)->homologous_filtered

homologous_gene_list<-function(mod){ 
  #this functions takes stable module assignments e.g. from clown and then combines all the other species and collates the data 
  #to obtain lists of genes shared between all 'homologous' modules
  #these genes can be though to represent conserved processes across species
  #annotating them shows which key processes have a high degree of co-regulation among species
  #select one column with stable annotation
  
  #homologous_filtered %>% filter(col.clown==mod)->one_col
  non_homologous_filtered %>% filter(col.clown==mod)->one_col #Use for non-homologus modules

  #get the list of 'homologus' columns in other species
  one_col %>% distinct(col.goby) %>% pull(col.goby)->goby_col_list
  one_col %>% distinct(col.danio) %>% pull(col.danio)->danio_col_list
  one_col %>% distinct(col.manini) %>% pull(col.manini)->manini_col_list
  one_col %>% distinct(col.grouper) %>% pull(col.grouper)->grouper_col_list
  
  #Here I get the genes from the above list of modules
  danio_col_get<-function(c1){danio_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(module==c1) %>% return()}
  
  manini_col_get<-function(c1){manini_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(module==c1) %>% return()}
  
  grouper_col_get<-function(c1){grouper_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(module==c1) %>% return()}
  
  goby_col_get<-function(c1){goby_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(module==c1) %>% return()}
  
  #I then combine all the genes from the list of modules above to select the genes that are present in all the modules. 
  #e.g. The orange clownfish module has significant overlap between darkgrey, tan, and green modules in zebrafish. While in manini, it has significant overlaps between darkturquoise, greenyellow, red, and green modules.
  #I take the genes from the zebrafish set and the manini set and combine them to only include genes that are present in both. I do this for the other two species.
  #The result is a list of genes that are, to an extent, co-expressed together. I say to an extent because, the same gene might not always be co-expressed together in the same module, in all species. 
  #For instance, look at the top ten genes in the common_all object. You'll see that all these genes are expressed together in the darkgrey module in zebrafish, but in manini some are expressed together in the greenyellow module, while some are expressed together in the red, or green module.  Essentially, this filtering approach captures genes that, on an average tend to be co-expressed together. This is expected considering they are different species with different developmental trajectories, but the fact that we can find a large degree of overlap between gene interactions across species highlights the presence of a common regulatory underpinning between orthologs. However, studying the deviations and specific modification of the network in each species will provide valuable information regarding the interplay of gene expression and regulatory evolution. 
  
inner_join(
    purrr::map(danio_col_list,danio_col_get) %>% list_rbind(),
    purrr::map(manini_col_list,manini_col_get) %>% list_rbind(), by = "gene", suffix = c(".danio", ".manini")) %>% 
    inner_join(purrr::map(grouper_col_list,grouper_col_get) %>% list_rbind(), by = "gene") %>% 
    inner_join(purrr::map(goby_col_list,goby_col_get) %>% list_rbind(), by = "gene", suffix = c(".grouper",".goby"))->common_all
  
  tibble(genes=common_all %>% inner_join(clown_orth_net$connectivity, by = "gene") %>% filter(module==mod)  %>% pull(gene)) %>% 
    mutate(mod=mod)%>% return()
  }

cols<-homologous_filtered %>% distinct(col.clown)
purrr::map(cols$col.clown, homologous_gene_list) %>% list_rbind() %>% distinct(genes, .keep_all = T)->homologous_genes
homologous_genes %>% distinct(mod)

homologous_genes %>% saveRDS("./RDS/homologous_genes.rds")

#Non-homologus, low preservation modules
clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(!module %in% (homologous_genes %>% distinct(mod) %>% pull(mod))) %>% distinct(module)->non_homologous_mods

homologous_modules %>% filter(col.clown %in% non_homologous_mods$module) %>% pivot_longer(contains("col"), names_to = "species.col", values_to = "col") %>% 
  pivot_longer(contains("jaccard"), names_to = "jaccard.comp", values_to = "jaccard.val") %>% 
  pivot_longer(contains("pres"),names_to = "pres.comp", values_to = "pres.val")->homologous_long_non_homologus

#filter out the top 30% non-homologous module comparisons
homologous_long_non_homologus %>% filter(jaccard.val >= quantile(homologous_long_non_homologus$jaccard.val,0.70)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(species.col, col) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = species.col, values_from =
                                                    col) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(col.goby, col.danio, col.manini, col.grouper, col.clown)) %>%
  distinct(col.goby, col.danio, col.manini, col.grouper, col.clown)->non_homologous_filtered

cols<-non_homologous_filtered %>% distinct(col.clown)
purrr::map(cols$col.clown, homologous_gene_list) %>% list_rbind() %>% distinct(genes, .keep_all = T)->non_homologous_genes
non_homologous_genes %>% distinct(mod)

non_homologous_genes %>% saveRDS("./RDS/non_homologous_genes.rds")

5.2 Average connectivity of homologus genes

The genes in the consereved network on an average have higher connectivity than the other genes not in the network. Therefore, they represent hub genes.

homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/homologous_genes.rds")

#non_homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/non_homologous_genes.rds")

    mutate(type="Yes"),
  clown_orth_net$connectivity %>% filter(!gene %in% homologous_genes$genes) %>% dplyr::select(gene, degree) %>%

wil_test_boot<-function(dat,species){
  rbind(
    dat$connectivity %>% filter(gene %in% homologous_genes$genes) %>% dplyr::select(gene, degree) %>% mutate(type="homologous"),
    dat$connectivity %>% filter(!gene %in% homologous_genes$genes) %>% dplyr::select(gene, degree) %>% mutate(type="other") %>% 
      slice_sample(n = 25)
  )->test_dat
  
  
  tibble(p.value=(
    wilcox.test(
      x = test_dat %>% filter(type=="homologous") %>% pull(degree),
      y = test_dat %>% filter(type=="other") %>% pull(degree),
      alternative = "greater")
    )$p.value,
         sp=paste0(species)
  ) %>% return()
}

rbind(
purrr::map(1:1000, ~wil_test_boot(dat = clown_orth_net, species = "Clownfish")) %>% 
  list_rbind(),
purrr::map(1:1000, ~wil_test_boot(dat = grouper_orth_net, species = "Grouper")) %>% 
  list_rbind(),
purrr::map(1:1000, ~wil_test_boot(dat = goby_orth_net, species = "Goby")) %>%
  list_rbind(),
purrr::map(1:1000, ~wil_test_boot(dat = manini_orth_net, species = "Manini")) %>% 
  list_rbind(),
purrr::map(1:1000, ~wil_test_boot(dat = danio_orth_net, species = "zebrafish")) %>% 
  list_rbind()
)->all_fish_wil_test_res

all_fish_wil_test_res %>% saveRDS("./RDS/all_fish_wil_test_res_connectivity_homologous.rds")

5.3 Preservation of conserved network modules

The modules in the conserved network had a high degree of preservation in all the species.

homologous_modules %>% filter(col.clown %in% homologous_genes$mod) %>% pivot_longer(c(clown.ref.pres.goby,clown.ref.pres.danio,clown.ref.pres.manini,
                                      clown.ref.pres.grouper,goby.ref.pres.clown,danio.ref.pres.clown,
                                      manini.ref.pres.clown,grouper.ref.pres.clown), 
                                    names_to = "comparisons", values_to = "module_pres") %>% 
  dplyr::count(module_pres) %>% mutate(n.per=n/sum(n)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=module_pres, y=n.per, fill=module_pres))+
  geom_col(color="black", linewidth=0.2)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#8C6BB1", "#2AA198", "#C97A5A"))+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)+
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(n.per,2)*100,"%"), y=n.per-0.03), size=3, color="white")+
  labs(x="Module\npreservation", y="Percentage in\npairwise comparisons")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size=8),
        legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey95"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey95"))->homo_pres_plots

homo_pres_plots

5.4 Gene copy-number of conserved network genes

Genes in the conserved network are not comprised of gene families that vary copy-number as compared to the full ortholog set. Suggesting that the developmental network likely does not have more redundancy (purely from a genetic perspective) than other sets of gene networks.

rbind(
  orth %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% homologous_genes$genes) %>% dplyr::count(Orthogroup) %>% mutate(type="Homologous"),
  orth %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% full_orths$Orthogroup & !Orthogroup %in% homologous_genes$genes) %>% 
    dplyr::count(Orthogroup)  %>% slice_sample(n=2000) %>% mutate(type="Non-homologous"))->ss_test

wilcox.test(x = ss_test %>% 
              filter(type=="Homologous") %>% pull(n) %>% log2(),
            
            y = ss_test %>% 
              filter(type=="Non-homologous") %>% 
              pull(n) %>% log2(), alternative = "two.sided")
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  ss_test %>% filter(type == "Homologous") %>% pull(n) %>% log2() and ss_test %>% filter(type == "Non-homologous") %>% pull(n) %>% log2()
## W = 1198414, p-value = 0.9238
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
ss_test %>%  ggplot(aes(y=log2(n), x=type, fill = type))+
  ggbeeswarm::geom_quasirandom(shape=21)+
  geom_boxplot(color="black", alpha=0.5, outliers = FALSE)+
  theme_bw()+  
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#EA5B15","#1AAEC0"))+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank())->gene_copy_number_homologous

gene_copy_number_homologous

6 Annotate the conserved modules

6.1 GO enrichment setup

## Identify the OGs in the homologous modules
orth %>% filter(sp=="Danio_rerio" & Orthogroup %in% danio_orth_net$connectivity$gene) %>%
  mutate(orths= str_remove(orths,"\\.[0-9]*"))->danio_macro_devo_net_genes #This will be the universe. 

clusterProfiler::bitr(danio_macro_devo_net_genes$orths, 
     fromType = "ENSEMBL",
     toType = "ENTREZID",
     OrgDb = org.Dr.eg.db) %>% 
  left_join(danio_macro_devo_net_genes, 
            by = c("ENSEMBL"="orths"))->danio_macro_devo_net_genes_annot

GO_entichment_test<-function(ont_type,mod,input_connectivity){
  
  danio_macro_devo_net_genes_annot %>% 
    filter(Orthogroup %in% (input_connectivity %>%
                              filter(module==mod) %>%
                              pull(gene)))->gene_set
  
  go_res <- enrichGO(
    gene          = gene_set$ENTREZID,
    universe      = unique(danio_macro_devo_net_genes_annot$ENTREZID),
    OrgDb         = org.Dr.eg.db,
    keyType       = "ENTREZID",
    ont           = ont_type,
    pAdjustMethod = "BH",
    pvalueCutoff  = 0.05,
    qvalueCutoff  = 0.05,
    readable      = TRUE)
  
  go_res_tbl <- as_tibble(go_res)
  go_res_tbl %>%
    arrange(p.adjust) %>%
    dplyr::select(ID, Description, p.adjust, qvalue, geneID) %>%
    head(20) %>% mutate(module=mod) %>%  return()
}
homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/homologous_genes.rds")
non_homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/non_homologous_genes.rds")

homologous_genes %>% distinct(mod) %>% pull(mod)->cols


purrr::map_dfr(cols, 
               ~GO_entichment_test(ont_type = "BP", 
                                   mod = .x,
                                   input_connectivity = clown_orth_net$connectivity),.progress = TRUE)->homologous_mods_BP_proc
homologous_mods_BP_proc %>% saveRDS("./03.Annotations/homologous_mods_BP_proc.rds")

homologous_modules %>% dplyr::select(col.clown, col.goby, col.danio, col.manini, col.grouper) %>% distinct(col.clown, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% filter(col.clown %in% unique(as.character((homologous_mods_BP_proc %>% list_rbind())$mod)))->mods_combs

  purrr::pmap(list(as.character(mods_combs$col.clown),
                   as.character(mods_combs$col.manini),
                   as.character(mods_combs$col.goby),

7 Expression trajectories of genes in homologous modules

In this section I explore the expression trajectories of the homologous genes in homologous modules across speices.


Across the five teleost species, the conserved network of 1,196 ortholog groups showed a broad functional distinction between components associated with core cellular processes and those involved in development and physiology. Core processes generally displayed gradual or plateau-like expression patterns, whereas developmental and physiological processes showed more stage-specific dynamics, often coinciding with peaks in thyroid hormone level across metamorphosis. These trajectories also reflected species-specific developmental events, including metabolic remodelling in clownfish and grouper, pelvic spine formation and regression in grouper, and increased neural, sensory, and nutrient-absorption activity during reef recruitment in manini. In zebrafish, which undergoes less pronounced post-embryonic remodelling, the distinction between the two functional classes was weaker.

Together, these results suggest that although the underlying co-expression architecture is conserved across teleosts, the timing and magnitude of its deployment vary among species, providing evidence for heterochrony and regulatory rewiring within a shared developmental network.

  samp.clown <- clown$dge_keep$samples %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("samples")
  
  clown$dge_keep$counts %>%
    edgeR::cpm(log = TRUE, prior.count = 1e-5, normalized.lib.sizes = TRUE) %>%
    reshape2::melt() %>%
    dplyr::rename(orths = Var1, samples = Var2, logCPM = value) %>%
    left_join(samp.clown, by = "samples") %>%
    dplyr::rename(stages = group) %>%
    summarise(mean_logCPM = mean(logCPM, na.rm = TRUE),
              .by = c(orths, stages)) %>% group_by(orths) %>%
    mutate(z.score = (mean_logCPM - mean(mean_logCPM))/sd(mean_logCPM)) %>%
    ungroup()->clown_zscore

8 T3 and MPI treatments

To experimentally test whether thyroid hormone can influence the conserved network, we clownfish exposed to a treatment of exogenous triiodothyronine (T3), a treatment of goitrogens (inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis) called MPI (methimazole, potassium perchlorate, iopanoic acid), and compared gene expression differences between with DMSO-treated controls.

8.1 Differential expression analysis

library(edgeR)

##T3
t3 <-read_csv("./RDS/T3_treatment_counts_raw.csv")

tibble(samples=colnames(t3 |> dplyr::select(-genes)),
       treatment=c(rep("control",10), rep("t3",10)))->t3.samples

cts.t3 <- t3 |> column_to_rownames("genes") |> as.matrix()

dge <- DGEList(
  counts = cts.t3,
  samples = t3.samples,
  genes = tibble(gene_id = rownames(cts.t3)))

design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + treatment,data = t3.samples)
keep<- filterByExpr(dge, min.count = 10, design)  
dge<-dge[keep, ,keep.lib.sizes =FALSE]
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge,method = "TMM")
t3.log_cpm <- edgeR::cpm(dge,log = TRUE,prior.count = 1e-5)
#limma::plotMDS(dge)

dge<-estimateDisp(dge, design, robust = T)
dge$common.dispersion
## [1] 0.0535263
#plotBCV(dge)
## Determining quasi likelihood
fit<-glmQLFit(dge, design, robust = T)
#head(fit$coefficients)
#plotQLDisp(fit)

## Differential expression analysis
con<-makeContrasts(treatmentt3-treatmentcontrol, levels = design)
qlf.t3<- glmQLFTest(fit,contrast=con)
ttgs<-topTags(qlf.t3,n = Inf) 
tibble(gene = ttgs$table$gene_id,logFC = ttgs$table$logFC,fdr = ttgs$table$FDR)->dge_res.t3
summary(decideTests(qlf.t3))

8.4 Fishers exact test for enrichment of DEGs in conserved network

The conserved network was enriched for differentially expressed genes in the T3 treatment, where network genes had 1.77-fold higher odds of differential expression than all other genes tested in the transcriptome (Fisher’s exact test). For the MPI treatment the conserved network was not enriched for differentially expressed genes.

dge_enrich<-function(dge_res, plot_dat){
  #dge_res=dge_res.t3
  #plot_dat=plot_dat.t3$gene
  
  de_results <- dge_res %>%
    mutate(significant = fdr < 0.05,
           gene_set = if_else(
             gene %in% plot_dat,
           "Conserved network",
           "Background"),
           gene_set = factor(
             gene_set,levels = c("Conserved network", "Background")))
  
  de_results |>       
    dplyr::count(gene_set, significant) |> 
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = significant,
      values_from = n,
      values_fill = 0)->test_matirx
  
  test_matrix <- de_results |> 
    dplyr::count(gene_set, significant) |> 
    complete(gene_set,
             significant,fill = list(n = 0)) |> 
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = significant,
      values_from = n,
      values_fill = 0) |> 
    arrange(gene_set) |> column_to_rownames("gene_set") %>%
    dplyr::select(`TRUE`, `FALSE`) |> as.matrix()
  
  enrichment_result <- fisher.test(
    test_matrix,alternative = "two.sided") %>% broom::tidy() 
  
  return(enrichment_result)
}
  
dge_enrich(dge_res = dge_res.t3, plot_dat = plot_dat.t3$gene)
dge_enrich(dge_res = dge_res.mpi, plot_dat = plot_dat.mpi$gene)

9 Endocrine candidates

Although thyroid hormone and corticosteroid signalling are central regulators of vertebrate post-embryonic development, candidate genes associated with these endocrine axes were largely absent from the conserved co-expression network. Instead, they were distributed across multiple modules within each species, suggesting that their expression relationships are more dynamic and lineage-specific than those of the conserved network components. These modules encompassed a wide range of functions, from core cellular processes such as DNA metabolism and Wnt signalling to developmental and physiological processes including extracellular matrix organisation and immune activity. Some endocrine-axis genes nevertheless retained similar functional contexts across species. For example, trh was consistently associated with modules involved in neural signalling in most species, reflecting its established neuroregulatory role, while duox was linked to immune-related modules in clownfish, goby, and grouper, consistent with its role in mucosal immunity. However, most candidate genes were embedded in modules with different functional associations across species. Together, these results suggest that although the thyroid hormone and corticosteroid axes are broadly conserved components of teleost post-embryonic development, the co-expression partners and biological processes through which they act have diverged among lineages, providing evidence for substantial flexibility and regulatory rewiring in their developmental context.

 make_lines_plot_for_the_candidates<-function(plot_data,sp){
   plot_dat <- plot_data  %>% 
     mutate(gene_name = na_if(gene_name, ""),
            gene_label = if_else(is.na(gene_name),
                                 orths,
                                 gene_name)) %>% 
     distinct(gene_label, stages, .keep_all = TRUE)
   
   label_dat <- plot_dat %>%
     group_by(Description, orths, candidate, gene_label) %>%
     arrange(stages, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
     slice_tail(n = 1) %>%
     ungroup()
   
   plot_dat %>% ggplot(aes(x=stages, y=z.score, group=orths, color=candidate))+
     facet_wrap(~Description)+
     geom_line()+
     ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = label_dat,aes(label = gene_label),
                              size = 2.5,nudge_x = 0.25,direction = "y",hjust = 0,
                              segment.size = 0.2,show.legend = FALSE)+
     scale_color_manual(values = c("#2BA09F","#A1562B"))+
     theme_bw()+
     theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 8),
           strip.text.x.top = element_text(size=5),
           strip.background = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = "#eee"))->p
   
   if (sp == "clown") {
     
     p <- p +
       annotate(
         geom = "rect",
         xmin = 3.5,
         xmax = 4.5,
         ymin = -Inf,
         ymax = Inf,
         fill = "#594BE4",
         alpha = 0.2)
     
   } else if (sp == "grouper") {
     
     p <- p +
       annotate(
         geom = "rect",
         xmin = 1.5,
         xmax = 2.5,
         ymin = -Inf,
         ymax = Inf,
         fill = "#594BE4",
         alpha = 0.2
       ) +
       annotate(
         geom = "rect",
         xmin = 5.5,
         xmax = 6.5,
         ymin = -Inf,
         ymax = Inf,
         fill = "#594BE4",
         alpha = 0.2
       )
  
    } else if (sp == "manini") {
     
     p <- p +
       annotate(
         geom = "rect",
         xmin = 0,
         xmax = 1.5,
         ymin = -Inf,
         ymax = Inf,
         fill = "#594BE4",
         alpha = 0.2
       )
     
   } else if (sp == "goby") {  
     
     p <- p 
     
   } else if (sp == "danio") {  
     
     p <- p +
       annotate(
         geom = "rect",
         xmin = 3.5,
         xmax = 4.5,
         ymin = -Inf,
         ymax = Inf,
         fill = "#594BE4",
         alpha = 0.2
       ) 
   }  
   
   return(p)
 }

10 Evolutionary dynamics of copy number variation

In this section I carry out the comparative evolutionary analysis using CAFE5. For the CAFE and the subsequent evolutionary analyses I excluded teleost lineages with additional lineage-specific WGDs because their genomes introduce extra paralogy, lineage-specific duplicate retention and loss, and extended rediploidisation dynamics, which can bias comparative estimates of copy-number evolution and regulatory divergence . The evolutionary analyses therefore focused on genomes sharing the same duplication background. Additionally, I selected species that were present in the phylogenetic tree from the Fish Tree of Life. The final list included 134 species and can be found in table S6.

#Get orthology data
orth<-readRDS("./04.Orthogroups/Orthologer_latest2.rds") %>% 
  mutate(sp=case_match(sp, "Goby" ~ "Rhinogobius_brunneus",

                           "Manini" ~ "Acanthurus_triostegus", 
                           "Gasterosteus_aculeatus_aculeatus" ~ "Gasterosteus_aculeatus", #fix this extra name
                       .default = sp))

pruned_tree<-drop.tip(pruned_tree,tip = "Carassius_langsdorfii")

I use CAFE5 to estimate evolutionary dynamics in copy-number evolution. First I ran a single-rate error corrected base model and a multi-rate model . The error model accounts for any non-biological factors such as genome sequencing and coverage differences, as well as gene family count estimation errors. I compared model fits using negative log-likelihood scores. The CAFE script can be found in the ‘Codes’ folder on zenodo.

non_homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/non_homologous_genes.rds")
homologous_genes<-readRDS("./RDS/homologous_genes.rds")

                            .default = "Non homologous")) #This contains data for the set of randomly selected genes that acts as the null.
#Use this random data for a null
seq_stats %>% filter(type=="Non homologous") %>% slice_head(n=1175) %>%   mutate(mod=paste0("random_mod", rep(1:25, each = 47))) %>% dplyr::rename("genes"="Orthogroup")->random_cafe
#it is 1175 because CAFE didn't converge for one of the modules.

This code chunk is used to make the input files for CAFE. They can be found on zenodo.

#Make CAFE input
make_cafe_input<-function(genelist, cols){
  specific_module<-genelist %>% filter(mod==cols)
  
  orth_gene_copy %>% filter(sp %in% no_WGD_tree$tip.label) %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% specific_module$genes) %>%
    dplyr::select(-c(Family, Order, SpecCode)) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = sp, values_from = no_of_gene_copies) %>%
    replace(is.na(.), 0) %>% mutate(`Family ID`=paste0("OG",Orthogroup), Desc="(null)") %>% 
    dplyr::select(c(Desc, `Family ID`, everything(), -Orthogroup)) %>% 
    write_tsv(paste0("./06.CAFE5/New_random/cafe_input_",cols,".tsv"))#change destination if needed
}

random_cafe %>% distinct(mod) %>% pull(mod)->cols
purrr::map(.x = cols, 
           ~make_cafe_input(genelist = random_cafe, cols = .x))

homologous_genes %>% distinct(mod) %>% pull(mod)->cols
purrr::map(.x = cols, 
           ~make_cafe_input(genelist = homologous_genes, cols = .x))

random_non_homologus_genes %>% distinct(mod) %>% pull(mod)->cols
purrr::map(.x = cols, 
           ~make_cafe_input(genelist = random_non_homologus_genes, cols = .x))

10.1 Results

Here I collect the outputs of CAFE and combine them into data frames. Adjust the file sources as per your system.

get_cafe_family_results<-function(cols,type){
  read_table(paste0("./06.CAFE5/",type,"/results_cafe_",cols,"/Multi_lambda_model_1/Base_family_results.txt"),
             skip = 1, col_names= c("genes","pval","is_sig"))->fam
  
  fam %>% mutate(mod=cols,
                 genes=str_remove_all(genes,"OG")) %>% return()
}

get_cafe_model_outputs<-function(cols,type){
  read_table(paste0("./06.CAFE5/",type,"/results_cafe_",cols,"/Base_model/Base_results.txt"),col_names = c("q","w","e","r","t","y"))->b
  
  tibble("neglogL"=b$y[1],
         "lambda1"=b$w[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "lambda2"=b$e[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "model_type"="base")->base_model
  
  read_table(paste0("./06.CAFE5/",type,"/results_cafe_",cols,"/Multi_lambda_model_1/Base_results.txt"),
             col_names=c("q","w","e","r","t","y"))->m1
  
  tibble("neglogL"=m1$y[1],
       "lambda1"=m1$w[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "lambda2"=m1$e[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "model_type"="multi_lambda_1")->multi_1
  
  read_table(paste0("./06.CAFE5/",type,"/results_cafe_",cols,"/Multi_lambda_model_2/Base_results.txt"),
             col_names=c("q","w","e","r","t","y"))->m2
  
  tibble("neglogL"=m2$y[1],
         "lambda1"=m2$w[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "lambda2"=m2$e[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "model_type"="multi_lambda_2")->multi_2
  
  read_table(paste0("./06.CAFE5/",type,"/results_cafe_",cols,"/Multi_lambda_model_3/Base_results.txt"),
           col_names=c("q","w","e","r","t","y"))->m3
  
  tibble("neglogL"=m3$y[1],
         "lambda1"=m3$w[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "lambda2"=m3$e[2] %>% str_remove_all(",") %>% as.numeric(),
         "model_type"="multi_lambda_3")->multi_3
  
 rbind(base_model, multi_1, multi_2, multi_3) %>% mutate(mod=cols) %>% 
    replace(is.na(.), 0) %>% return()

}

10.1.1 Connectivity of the fast evolving genes

Here I check whether the high turnover genes estimated by CAFE have different connectivity than low turnover genes form the conserved network.
The connectivity of the high turnover conserved network genes is not significantly different from all the other, low-turnover genes in the conserved network. Therefore, the fast evolving genes are not hyper-hubs.

wil_test_boot<-function(dat,species){
  rbind(
    dat$connectivity %>% filter(gene %in% (cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(is_sig=="y" & mod_type=="Homologous") %>% pull(genes))) %>% dplyr::select(gene, degree) %>% mutate(type="homologous"),
    dat$connectivity %>% filter(gene %in% homologous_genes$genes & !gene %in% (cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(is_sig=="y" & mod_type=="Homologous") %>% pull(genes))) %>% dplyr::select(gene, degree) %>% mutate(type="other") %>% 
      slice_sample(n=170)
  )->test_dat
  
  
  tibble(p.value=(
    wilcox.test(
      x = test_dat %>% filter(type=="homologous") %>% pull(degree),
      y = test_dat %>% filter(type=="other") %>% pull(degree),
      alternative = "two.sided")
    )$p.value,
         sp=paste0(species)
  ) %>% return()
}

10.1.4 Expansion and contraction of gene families

Here I plot the relative expansion and contraction of homologous gene families estimated by CAFE. We see that there are different points of expansion/contraction along the tree occurring at different nodes. The highest expansion occurred at the root of teleost as a result of the teleost specific whole genome duplication (3R).
The expansions and contractions are all significant.

10.1.4.2 Specific nodes

There were many lineage specific points of expansions and contractions. For example, at the base of the teleost radiation there was extensive expansion primarily in gene families related to synaptic signalling and nervous system development. At the base of anguilliformes, there were expansions in genes related to translation and synaptic signalling. Another point of expansion was at the base of scombriformes which involved the expansion of the immune system and synaptic signalling genes. In contrast, at the base of siluriformes there were major contractions in genes related to synaptic signalling. Another major point of contraction was at the base of syngnathiformes, which involved contractions in genes related to the immune system and synaptic signalling. There were multiple instances of expansions and contractions at the base of cichliformes, with a major expansion in gene families related to the immune system, and a loss in families related to synaptic signalling and brushborder epithelium development. The full list of high turnover genes can be found in table S3.

10.1.4.3 Proportion of turnover between homologous and random genes

Of all the gene families in the conserved network, 14% (170 out of 1196) had significant evidence of high turnover. However, the proportion of gene families with evidence of high turnover differed significantly (two-sided Fisher’s exact test P = 0.0002, odds ratio 1.6) between the conserved network and null network, with the conserved network comprising a higher proportion of high turnover gene families.
Doing the test without the re-sampling gives a significant difference (reported P above) in proportions between homologous and non-homologous networks. I perform the re-sampling to ensure there is consistency in the data sampling and results.

## 
##  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data
## 
## data:  .
## p-value = 0.0002719
## alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  1.234073 2.088594
## sample estimates:
## odds ratio 
##    1.60308
fisher_boot_test<-function(){
  rbind(
    cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(mod_type=="Homologous") %>% 
      slice_sample(n=500,replace = TRUE),
    cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(mod_type=="Non homologous") %>% 
      slice_sample(n=500,replace = TRUE)) %>% 
    dplyr::count(is_sig, mod_type) %>% 
    pivot_wider(names_from = is_sig, 
                values_from = n, 
                values_fill = 0) %>% dplyr::select(y,n) %>%
    as.matrix() %>% fisher.test()->test_res
  
  tibble(pval=test_res$p.value,
         odds=test_res$estimate) %>% return()
}

11 Selection analysis

To understand how the conserved network evolved in teleosts I ran several molecular evolution models to infer selection patterns in coding sequence alignments across 133 teleost fish species and the spotted gar, Lepiosteous oculatus, as the outgroup.
I compared the selection estimates of genes in the conserved network to an equal sized random set of genes not in the network which served as our null set, similar to CAFE. I ran several evolutionary models implemented in the HyPhy suite of models.
The analyses on coding sequence evolution indicates that most protein residues in both the sets (from the conserved network and null set) are under strong evolutionary constraint, with occasional bouts of episodic diversifying selection taking place in a few branches. However this general trend differs slightly between the two sets. Genes belonging to the conserved network show a slightly higher proportion of sites under purifying selection, as well as a greater number of branches with evidence of diversifying selection. Although these differences are statistically significant, they are associated with relatively small effect sizes.

Prior to running analyses I checked for any group level differences in gene length or orthology copy number between the conserved and null class. I found no evidence of differences in average gene length or copy number between these two classes (bootstrapped two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected P > 0.2). Therefore, the difference in gene length or copy number did not confound our estimates of selection between the two groups.

11.2 Global dN/dS using MG94 model

First I used a standard MG94 selection model to get a global estimate of dN/dS estimated from the entire tree. Using this global estimate I found no evidence for difference in dN/dS between genes in the conserved network versus the null, non-conserved gene set. The global MG94 is a highly conservative estimate that rarely captures selective regimes at the branch and site level.

#Parse the JSON file from HyPhy
fitmg94_json_parse<-function(orth) {
  library(jsonlite)
  f<-read_json(paste0("./10.HyPhy/MG94/",orth,"_fitmg94.local.json"))
  
  tibble(
    Orthogroup=orth,
    omega=f$fits$`Standard MG94`$`Rate Distributions`$`non-synonymous/synonymous rate ratio`,
    omega_ci_lb=f$fits$`Standard MG94`$`Confidence Intervals`$`non-synonymous/synonymous rate ratio`$LB,
    omega_ci_ub=f$fits$`Standard MG94`$`Confidence Intervals`$`non-synonymous/synonymous rate ratio`$UB,
    p_val=f$`test results`$`non-synonymous/synonymous rate ratio`$`p-value`,
    lrt=f$`test results`$`non-synonymous/synonymous rate ratio`$LRT)
}

rbind(
  homologous_genes$genes %>%
  purrr::map(safely(fitmg94_json_parse)) %>%
  purrr::map("result") %>%       
  compact() %>% 
  list_rbind() %>% mutate(type="Homologous"),
  
  (genes_needed %>% distinct(Orthogroup) %>% 
    filter(!Orthogroup %in% homologous_genes$genes))$Orthogroup %>%
  purrr::map(safely(fitmg94_json_parse)) %>%
  purrr::map("result") %>%       
  compact() %>% 
  list_rbind() %>% mutate(type="Non Homologous")) %>%
      mutate(pval_adj=p.adjust(p_val,method = "BH"))->fitmg94_res
fitmg94_res<-readRDS("./RDS/fitmg94_res.rds")

  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

test_wil<-function(){
  
  rbind(fitmg94_res %>% filter(pval_adj < 0.05) %>% slice_sample(n=200))->test_dat
  
  wilcox.test(x=test_dat %>% filter(type=="Homologous") %>% pull(omega) %>% log2(),
              y=test_dat %>% filter(type=="Non Homologous") %>% pull(omega) %>% log2(),
              alternative = "two.sided")->wil.res
  
  tibble(pval=wil.res$p.value,
         test=wil.res$alternative) %>% return()
  }

purrr::map(1:1000, ~test_wil()) %>% list_rbind() %>% mutate(padj=p.adjust(pval,"BH"))->global_sel_diff
global_sel_diff %>% summarise(mean_padj=mean(padj))
global_sel_diff %>% summarise(median_padj=median(padj))

11.3 FUBAR

I estimated dN/dS on a per-site basis using the FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian Approximation) approach. FUBAR provides site-wise estimates for purifying and diversifying selection regimes, or uncertain sites with low evidence for either regime. The analyses revealed that a majority of the sites in genes from the conserved network evolve under a purifying selection with very few sites evolving under diversifying selection (Fig 2B). The same was observed for the sites in genes from the non-conserved null set. This suggests that these orthologs are generally under high evolutionary constraint at the site level. However, the distribution of evolutionary regimes differs significantly between the two groups (χ² = 651.4, P < 2.2×10⁻¹⁶) with the genes in the conserved network having slightly higher proportion of sites under purifying selection and lower proportion of genes under diversifying selection, as compared to the null set. Although the difference between the groups is significant, the effect size is small (Cramer’s V = 0.019).

#Parse HyPhy output
list.files("./10.HyPhy/FUBAR/") %>% 
  str_remove_all("_cds_treeinput.fa.FUBAR.json")->og

fubar_json_parse<- function(orth) {
  f<-read_json(paste0("./10.HyPhy/FUBAR/",orth,"_cds_treeinput.fa.FUBAR.json"),
               simplifyVector = )
  headers <- map_chr(f$MLE$headers,1)
  rows <- f$MLE$content$`0`
  rows <- purrr::modify(rows, ~ modify(.x, ~ if (is.null(.x)) 0 else .x))
  sites <- f$`data partitions`$`0`$coverage
  
  purrr::map(.x = rows, 
      ~as_tibble(setNames(as.list(.x), c(headers,"q1","q2")))) %>% list_rbind() %>% 
    mutate(sites=seq(1:length(sites[[1]])),
           Orthogroup=orth) %>% 
    dplyr::select(Orthogroup,sites, everything()) %>% 
    return()
}

rbind(
  homologous_genes$genes %>%
    purrr::map(safely(fubar_json_parse)) %>%
    purrr::map("result") %>%       
    compact() %>% 
    list_rbind() %>% mutate(type="Homologous"),
  
  (genes_needed %>% distinct(Orthogroup) %>% 
     filter(!Orthogroup %in% homologous_genes$genes))$Orthogroup  %>%
    purrr::map(safely(fubar_json_parse)) %>%
    purrr::map("result") %>%       
    compact() %>% 
    list_rbind() %>% mutate(type="Non homologous")
)->fubar_res

11.4 BUSTED

Next I ran the BUSTED (Branch-Site Unrestricted Statistical Test for Episodic Diversification) model to test for selection at the gene level. BUSTED fits a codon model with multiple rates classes and tests for evidence of diversifying selection occurring at at least one site in at least one branch in the tree (an episode of diversification). The analysis revealed branches with evidence for episodic diversifying selection in genes from both the conserved network and null set. However, the conserved network genes had a higher proportion of branches with evidence of episodic diversifying selection than the null set (two-sided Fisher’s exact test P = 0.011, odds ratio = 1.22).

busted_json_parse<- function(orth) {
  library(jsonlite)
  f<-read_json(paste0("./10.HyPhy/BUSTED/",orth, "_cds_treeinput.fa.BUSTED.json"),
               simplifyVector = TRUE)
  
  tibble(Orthogroup=orth,
         p_value=as.numeric(f$`test results`$`p-value`),
         lrt=as.numeric(f$`test results`$LRT),
         no_of_branches=length(f$tested$`0`)) %>% 
    return()
}


rbind(
  homologous_genes$genes %>%
    purrr::map(safely(busted_json_parse)) %>%
    purrr::map("result") %>%       
    compact() %>% 
    list_rbind() %>% 
    mutate(type="Homologous"),
  
  (genes_needed %>% distinct(Orthogroup) %>% 
     filter(!Orthogroup %in% homologous_genes$genes))$Orthogroup %>% 
    purrr::map(safely(busted_json_parse)) %>%
    purrr::map("result") %>%       
    compact() %>% 
    list_rbind() %>% 
    mutate(type="Non homologous")
) %>% mutate(p_adj=p.adjust(p_value, "BH"))->busted_res

12 PGLMM

Here I investigated the relationship between copy number variation of the high turnover gene families and phenotypic variation in multiple traits across teleosts. Using phylogenetic generalised linear mixed model (PGLMM) I model the trait of interest as a response variable with the scores of the first two principal components (PC) of a phylogenetic PCA of gene copy variation as the predictors, and phylogeny as the group level effect (random effect). The traits of interest were maximum age, age of maturity, average water temperature of sampled population, trophic level, von Bertalanffy growth coefficient (rate at which an organism approaches its maximum theoretical size), body shape, demersal habitat type, aspect ratio of caudal fin height divided by area (proxy for swimming performance), and length of lower jaw. The data is primarily from the FishLife package, with has curated estimates from FishBase. The traits of interest are both categorical and continuous.
Details regarding transformation and units of measurements can be found in Table S4.

12.1 Load the data

To improve the interpretation of the model outputs and minimise the risk of spurious associations, I evaluated several aspects of both model fit and the underlying data. For all models with statistically significant parameter estimates, I first examined model diagnostics to confirm proper convergence. I then inspected the plotted data and the phylogenetic PCA to verify that the observed relationships were not driven by a small number of outlier species occupying extreme positions in the phylomorphic space. Lastly I checked the expression of the genes using data from the Bgee gene expression database to determine whether the genes are expressed in the relevant tissues. I also used data from the Zebrafish Information Network (ZFIN) to examine the unique phenotypic terms associated with genetic perturbation (knockdowns, mutation screens, and morpholino experiments) of genes comprising the modules in Danio rerio (41). The ZFIN database provides a wide array of expertly curated cross-referenced genetic and genomics data that is routinely used to study gene functions (41). For the phenotypes, I focus on genes making up entire modules in order to capture the functional outcome of all interaction partners. Applying these criteria, I identified evidence for several relationships between gene copy number variation and ecological or morphological traits. For brevity I focus on three noteworthy cases in the main manuscript.

#log of maximum age (years)
 brms_model_age<-function(col){
   library(brms)
   
   cafe_genefamily_outs<-cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(is_sig=="y" & mod_type=="Homologous")
   #lead the genecopy data
   orth_gene_copy %>% filter(Orthogroup %in% (cafe_genefamily_outs %>% filter(mod==col) %>% 
                                                pull(genes))) %>% 
     filter(sp %in% pglmm_tree$tip.label) %>% 
     dplyr::select(-c(Family, Order, SpecCode)) %>% 
     pivot_wider(names_from = Orthogroup, values_from = no_of_gene_copies) %>% 
     replace(is.na(.), 0) %>% filter(sp %in% shapes_dat$sp)->sp_genes_wide
   #colnames(sp_genes_wide)<-c("sp", paste0("gene",seq(1:(ncol(sp_genes_wide)-1))))
   
   expr_scaled<-sp_genes_wide %>% column_to_rownames("sp")->pca_dat_gene
   scale(pca_dat_gene, center = FALSE,scale = TRUE)->pca_dat_gene
   pca_gene_pca <- phytools::phyl.pca(pglmm_tree, pca_dat_gene, method = "lambda", mode = "corr")
   pca_gene <- as.data.frame(pca_gene_pca$S) %>% dplyr::rename_with(~paste0(.,".cpy")) %>% 
     rownames_to_column("sp")
   
   #Get this data from FishLife
   data(FishBase_and_Morphometrics)
   tibble(log_age=FishBase_and_Morphometrics$Y_ij[,1]) %>%
     mutate(sp=(rownames(FishBase_and_Morphometrics$Y_ij) %>% str_replace_all(" ","_"))) %>%
     drop_na() %>% filter(sp %in% no_WGD_tree$tip.label) %>% 
     summarise(mean_log_age=mean(log_age), .by = "sp")->fishbase_age_dat
   
   #join the datasets
   left_join(pca_gene,fishbase_age_dat) %>% drop_na()->model_dat
   
   #Prune the pglmm tree
   pglmm_tree_fishbase<-drop.tip(pglmm_tree,pglmm_tree$tip.label[-match(model_dat$sp, pglmm_tree$tip.label)])
   is.rooted(pglmm_tree_fishbase)
   is.ultrametric(pglmm_tree_fishbase)
   #Must pass namecheck
   geiger::name.check(pglmm_tree_fishbase,model_dat %>% column_to_rownames("sp"))
   
   #plots to visualise response and predictors
   ggarrange(
     model_dat %>% 
       ggplot(aes(x=PC1.cpy, y=mean_log_age))+
       geom_point(shape=21, fill="#8BAE06", size=3)+
       geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,colour = "#F0710F",show.legend = TRUE)+
       theme_linedraw(),
     
     model_dat %>% 
       ggplot(aes(x=PC2.cpy, y=mean_log_age))+
       geom_point(shape=21, fill="#8BAE06", size=3)+
       geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,colour = "#F0710F")+
       theme_linedraw(),
     nrow = 1, ncol = 2)->age_plots
   
   #Phylogenetic covariance matrix
   A<-MCMCglmm::inverseA(pglmm_tree_fishbase,scale = TRUE,nodes = "TIPS")
   A<-A$Ainv
   #Priors
   priors_age<-get_prior(mean_log_age ~  
                           PC1.cpy + PC2.cpy +(1 |gr(sp, cov = A)),  
                           data = model_dat,
                           data2   = list(A = A),
                           family = gaussian())
   #Model
   model_brms_age <- brm(mean_log_age ~  PC1.cpy + PC2.cpy +(1 |gr(sp, cov = A)),
     data = model_dat,
     data2   = list(A = A),
     prior = priors_age,
     family = gaussian(),
     chains = 4, 
     cores = 4,
     iter = 5000, 
     warmup = 1000,
     backend = "cmdstanr",
     control = list(adapt_delta=0.999, max_treedepth = 12)
   )
   
   
   return(list(pca_gene_pca=pca_gene_pca,
               age_plots=age_plots,
               model_brms_age=model_brms_age))
 }
